fluxkv Golden Benchmark

Whole matrix at a glanceT1–T20 · L1–L20

Every workload on one page

Maximum throughput from the T row. Space and write amplification come from the same run. p99 comes from the matching L row paced at 25% and 50% of that maximum. Bars share one scale within each value size.

The workloads

Every workload is uniform random: each operation picks its key uniformly at random, with no hot set. Inserts draw new keys in a scrambled order, so they also land uniformly across the key space.

Read
GET of a uniformly random existing key. In memory rows serve every GET from the Document Cache; on disk rows turn it off, so each GET goes through the index to the data on disk.
Insert
SET of a new key, added on top of the preloaded data, so the store grows during the run.
Overwrite
SET of a uniformly random existing key, replacing its value. The store stays the same size and compaction reclaims the old versions.
Non-blind write
The SET first looks up the existing key, which costs an index read.
Blind write
The SET is written without looking up the old value.
Durable
A SET is acknowledged once the shared write-ahead log reports it persisted. Non-durable SETs are acknowledged before that.
Document Cache
The fluxkv server's in-memory cache of whole documents (key and value), in front of magma and its block cache.

Space against write amplification

space amp = du ÷ keys × (12 B + value) · write amp = device bytes ÷ bytes ingested · color = durability · filled = non-blind · ring = blind

At 8 B the per-key overhead (seq record, key index entry, metadata) is several times the 20 B payload, so both figures grow. Blind 8 B overwrites reach 16× space because their garbage is only found by compaction.

Read throughputT1 · T2 · T11 · T12

Reads: from memory and from disk

Squares show read IOs per GET, from device read counts divided by GETs served. One full square means every GET costs exactly one IO.

In-memory rows run 80 IO threads with the client shape that peaks each: 1 KB reads are CPU-bound and peak at a shallow pipeline, 8 B reads need ~164K requests in flight. Both keep the 100 µs response-coalescing timer.

Memory against dataE rows

Residency: how much of the data fits in memory

Memory is the 16 GiB quota (direct IO), 10.9 GB of it block cache; in-memory rows add a 32 GiB Document Cache. The index is 6.7 GB at 100M keys.

Index residency: one dataset, less memory

100M keys × 1 KB, the same data in every row; only the block cache shrinks (--write-cache-ratio). Memory per key is block cache ÷ 100M keys.*

* Data resident is memory given (the 16 GiB quota at 100%; block cache plus the 324 MB pinned memtables below that) ÷ the data directory's size on disk. Index resident divides the cache by uncompressed key-tree leaves (44 B per key) plus index blocks, so it understates residency: leaves are LZ4-compressed in the cache, and at full residency the working set is about 33 B per key.

What was run, and how

Two value sizes, each with two read rows and eight write rows (insert or overwrite × durable or not × blind or non-blind). Each throughput row T has a latency row L paced from its result, plus four two-hour S rows. All keys are 12 B, uniform, in scrambled order, with a 1 KB seqIndex block.

  • Kernel lock contentionThe kernel spin-lock share of CPU stayed under 2% on every row.
  • Response-coalescing timerMAGMA_FLUSH_DELAY_US=100 rounds up to a ~1 ms epoll tick on a quiet loop, so it is off for every row except the saturated in-memory reads.
  • Insert rows grow the storeA 900 s 1 KB insert adds 1.2–1.2B keys and ends near 1.6 TB on disk. Throughput is the average over that growth.
  • Same-box pairsEach durable and non-durable pair ran on one box: T3–T6 on .51, T7–T10 on .52, S1–S4 on .53.
  • In-memory latency rowsL1 and L11 are paced from 16.6M and 62.0M get/s. L11 at 50% and 75% is limited by the latency client itself.
  • MemoryRSS is the server's resident set at the end of each run, with jemalloc untuned.
  • Box hygienefstrim /data before every load; performance governor and aio limits persisted on all four boxes.
